modules.title: Content Systems That Scale
modules.description: Build a repeatable content process you can sell as a monthly service. Covers calendars, repurposing, and handing over work a client can review quickly.

lessons.title: One Idea, Many Places

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most businesses producing content are inventing something new every time. That is why they run out of energy in about six weeks, and why they keep hiring people to restart it.

The businesses that keep going are not more creative. They are reusing a small number of ideas in different shapes, and that difference is a system you can build and sell.

blocks.heading: Reuse Is Not Repetition
blocks.bodyHtml:
The fear is that saying the same thing twice looks lazy. In practice almost nobody sees everything you publish.

Writing a new topic for every post, every week, forever.

Taking one strong idea and giving it five shapes: the short version, the example, the counter-argument, the checklist, the story behind it.

Same idea, five entries, and each one reaches people the others missed.

blocks.text: Almost nobody sees everything you publish. Repetition is a fear, not a risk.

blocks.heading: The Shapes That Work
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The claim — the idea stated plainly in two lines
  • The example — one real case where it happened
  • The counter — the common belief it contradicts
  • The how — steps someone can follow today
  • The story — how you learned it, including getting it wrong

Five shapes from one idea. A month of content is now four ideas, which is a completely different task from twenty.

blocks.question: A client wants twenty posts a month and worries about running out of things to say. Best structure?

options.label: Twenty separate topics, planned in advance across the whole quarter.
Four ideas a month, each written in five different shapes and formats.
Whatever is topical that week, decided a few days before publishing.
Ten topics, each published twice with slightly different wording used.

blocks.successBody: Four ideas is a manageable creative task; twenty is not, which is why calendars collapse. Five shapes per idea produces genuine variety in form while keeping the thinking load small enough to sustain.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which structure is still workable in month six, not just month one.

blocks.heading: Harvest, Do Not Invent
blocks.bodyHtml:
The ideas already exist inside the business. They are in support emails, sales calls, the questions asked before every purchase, and the objections that come up weekly.

Twenty minutes in a client's inbox produces more usable material than a day of brainstorming — and it comes phrased in the customer's own words, which is exactly what you need anyway.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take one idea you believe about your own work and write it as a claim.
Now write the same idea as an example, a counter, a how-to and a story.
Notice which shape was hardest — that is usually the most valuable one.
List the five questions you get asked most: those are five more ideas.

blocks.heading: Sell the System, Not the Posts
blocks.bodyHtml:
Posts are a commodity and get priced like one. A system — idea harvesting, five shapes, a monthly calendar and a review step — is a service, and it is the thing that makes a retainer make sense.

It is also more honest. What the client actually needs is to stop running out of things to say, and that is what you are solving.

blocks.body: Content collapses when every piece needs a new idea. Take four ideas a month and give each five shapes — claim, example, counter, how-to, story. Harvest the ideas from support emails and sales questions rather than inventing them, and sell the system rather than the posts.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: building a calendar the client can actually keep to.

lessons.title: A Calendar That Survives Contact With Reality

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Almost every content calendar is built in an optimistic hour and abandoned within a month. The plan was not wrong; it was designed for a version of the week that never happens.

A calendar that survives is built around the worst realistic week, not the best one — and that single change is what makes it still be running in month six.

blocks.heading: Plan for the Bad Week
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ambition at the planning stage is what causes collapse later.

«Five posts a week, plus a newsletter and a monthly long-form piece.»

«Two posts a week and one newsletter a month, produced in a single batch on the first Monday.»

The second one is boring and still running in December. Consistency at a low volume beats intensity that stops.

blocks.text: A calendar built for your best week is a calendar built for four weeks.

blocks.heading: Batch, Do Not Trickle
blocks.bodyHtml:
• One session for ideas — harvest four, decide the shapes
  • One session for drafting — all of them, in one context
  • One session for editing and scheduling — the whole month at once

Three focused sessions beat twenty interruptions, because most of the cost of a piece is starting it. Batching pays that cost once.

blocks.question: A client keeps missing their own publishing schedule. What is the most likely fix?

options.label: A stricter schedule with clear deadlines and reminders for each piece.
Halve the volume and produce everything in one batch session monthly.
Add another person to the process so the work is shared between two.
Move to a different platform where the audience is easier to reach.

blocks.successBody: Missed schedules are almost always a volume problem wearing a discipline costume. Less work, produced in one sitting, is what people actually keep doing — and consistency at low volume outperforms bursts.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about whether the problem is willpower or the amount of work being planned.

blocks.heading: Two Weeks Ahead, Always
blocks.bodyHtml:
Keep a fortnight of finished content scheduled at all times. Not a month — that is too much stock to keep fresh — and not three days, which is where panic lives.

The buffer absorbs illness, holidays and busy weeks, and it is what turns publishing from a recurring emergency into something that just happens.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write the smallest publishing schedule you would be embarrassed to admit to.
Halve it once more, then commit to that for three months.
Block one batch session per month in the calendar as a real appointment.
Build a two-week buffer before publishing anything at all.

blocks.heading: Review Once a Month, Not Daily
blocks.bodyHtml:
Checking numbers after every post produces anxiety and no information — the variance between individual pieces is mostly noise.

Look once a month at which ideas travelled and which shapes worked. That is a pattern you can act on, and it fits neatly into the same session where you plan the next four ideas.

blocks.body: Calendars fail because they are built for the best week. Halve the volume, batch production into three sessions, keep a two-week buffer of finished pieces, and review results monthly rather than daily. Boring and still running beats ambitious and abandoned.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: reporting on content in a way that leads to more work.

lessons.title: Reporting So the Client Sees the Value

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Content retainers are cancelled more often for invisibility than for poor results. The work happened, the numbers were fine, and nobody inside the business could say what it had done.

A short monthly report fixes that. It is fifteen minutes of work and it is frequently what decides whether the arrangement continues.

blocks.heading: Report Meaning, Not Metrics
blocks.bodyHtml:
A wall of numbers puts the interpretation back on the client, who will not do it.

«Impressions 14,300, engagement 2.1%, clicks 190, follows +38.»

«The delivery-times post did three times the usual traffic — people are still deciding based on that. Worth a second piece and a line on the product page.»

The second is the same data with the thinking done, which is the part they are paying for.

blocks.text: A report full of numbers hands the client homework. A report with one recommendation hands them a decision.

blocks.heading: Four Lines Is Enough
blocks.bodyHtml:
• What went out — counts, one line
  • What worked — the best piece and, briefly, why
  • What that suggests — one observation about the audience
  • What you recommend next — one concrete action

Four lines, sent on the same date every month. That predictability is itself reassuring, and it is what makes you feel like part of the business rather than a supplier.

blocks.question: A month's results are mediocre — nothing performed particularly well. What do you report?

options.label: Report the numbers plainly and note that this month was a quiet one.
Say what the flat month rules out, and name the one thing to test next.
Highlight the best-performing piece to keep the tone of the report positive.
Skip the report this month and send a fuller one when results recover.

blocks.successBody: A flat month is information: it eliminates possibilities. Saying what it rules out and naming the next test keeps you in the role of someone thinking about the business, which is exactly what survives a bad month.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which response is still useful to the client when the news is not good.

blocks.heading: Agree the Measure First
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ask at the start what would make this worth doing — enquiries, sales, fewer support emails — and report against that.

Otherwise you report reach while they were quietly counting enquiries, and the arrangement ends with both sides thinking the other misunderstood something obvious.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your four-line report template with blanks for the specifics.
Add the question you will ask about what counts as success.
Set a fixed monthly date and keep it even in bad months.
Practise on any content you have made, including your own.

blocks.heading: Show the Thing They Can Reuse
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once a month, hand over something they can use elsewhere: the customer question that keeps appearing, the phrase that performed, the objection nobody had noticed.

That is worth more than the posts themselves, because it feeds their sales and product decisions — and it is why the retainer stops being a line item they periodically reconsider.

blocks.body: Retainers end because value became invisible, not because results were poor. Send four lines every month on the same date: what went out, what worked, what it suggests, what to do next. Agree the measure up front, and hand over one insight they can use elsewhere.
blocks.nextTeaser: You now have the full writing path: the job behind the words, the voice, the format, the system and the report.

modules.title: Visuals With AI
modules.description: Produce images that look intentional instead of generated. Covers style consistency, revisions, and delivering files a client can actually use.

lessons.title: Why Generated Images Look Generated

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
People can now spot AI images at a glance, and they have started to associate that look with a business that did not try very hard. That is a real commercial problem, not a matter of taste.

The giveaway is rarely a technical flaw. It is that the image looks like it was made for nobody in particular — which is exactly what happens when nothing specific was asked for.

blocks.heading: The Default Look
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ask for something general and you get the average of everything: shallow depth of field, glossy lighting, a symmetrical composition, colours that belong to no brand.

«A professional photo of a coffee shop.»

«Morning light through a side window, one cup on a scratched wooden counter, shot from standing height, muted greens.»

The second one describes a decision. The first one asks for a consensus, and consensus is what looks generated.

blocks.text: Images look generated when nobody made a decision about them.

blocks.heading: Four Decisions Worth Making
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Light — where it comes from and what time of day it implies
  • Position — where the viewer is standing, and how far away
  • Imperfection — a worn surface, an off-centre object, something real
  • Palette — the brand's actual colours, named, not implied

Four decisions turn a stock-looking render into something that could plausibly belong to one business rather than any business.

blocks.question: A client says the images «look like AI». Which change helps most?

options.label: Generate at a higher resolution so that the fine detail is much sharper.
Specify the light, the camera position and one imperfect real detail.
Try a different image tool that has a reputation for realistic output.
Add more descriptive adjectives about quality and professionalism.

blocks.successBody: The generated look comes from unmade decisions, not from resolution or tooling. Naming the light, the viewpoint and one imperfect detail is what makes an image feel photographed rather than assembled.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what actually differs between a real photograph and a default render.

blocks.heading: Match the Business, Not the Trend
blocks.bodyHtml:
A tone that suits a fashion brand actively harms a plumber. Generated images drift toward whatever looks impressive in general, which is often wrong for the specific business paying you.

Look at their existing photos, their premises, their customers. The image should look like it came from the same world, and that is a research task before it is a generation task.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a real local business and describe one image using the four decisions.
Generate it, then generate the vague version of the same request.
Put both next to a real photo from that business and compare.
Note which decision made the biggest difference — usually the light.

blocks.heading: Edit After Generating
blocks.bodyHtml:
Almost nothing should ship exactly as generated. A crop, a colour adjustment towards the brand palette, and removing the one strange detail takes five minutes.

That pass is most of the visible difference between a freelancer's work and something the client could have produced themselves in a browser tab — which matters, because they know they could.

blocks.body: Generated images look generated because no decisions were made. Specify the light, the viewpoint, one imperfection and the real palette, match the business rather than a trend, and always edit afterwards — a crop and a colour pass are what separate paid work from a free render.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: why consistency, not quality, is what clients are actually buying.

lessons.title: Consistency Is the Whole Job

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
A client can produce one good image on their own now. What they cannot produce is forty images that look like they belong to the same company.

That is the actual service, and it is worth noticing early, because it changes what you practise and what you sell. Nobody is paying for your best single image.

blocks.heading: One Image Is a Sample, Forty Are a Brand
blocks.bodyHtml:
Consistency is what makes a set of images read as intentional.

Forty striking images, each in a slightly different style.

Forty ordinary images with the same light, palette, framing and level of detail.

The second set looks professional even when no individual image is remarkable. The first looks like someone was experimenting in public.

blocks.text: Nobody is paying for your best image. They are paying for your fortieth to match your first.

blocks.heading: What Has to Stay Fixed
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Palette — the same handful of colours, named as values
  • Light direction and quality — soft from the left, every time
  • Framing distance — how close the subject sits in frame
  • Level of realism — photographic or illustrated, never both in a set

Write these down once as a recipe. Reusing the recipe is the job; inventing a new one for each image is why sets drift.

blocks.question: A client needs twenty images for a product range. What matters most?

options.label: That each image is as visually striking and memorable as possible.
That all twenty share the same light, palette, framing and realism.
That every image is generated at the maximum resolution available.
That the set covers as many different styles as the products allow.

blocks.successBody: A range is read as a set, not as individual pictures. Shared light, palette and framing make twenty ordinary images look deliberate, while twenty striking but unrelated ones look like a collection of experiments.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about how the images will be seen — one at a time, or together on a page?

blocks.heading: Build the Recipe First
blocks.bodyHtml:
Spend the first hour of a set producing one image you are happy with, then write down exactly what produced it — every specification, in order.

The remaining nineteen are variations on that recipe, changing only the subject. This is also why the second project for the same client is far more profitable than the first.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Make one image you are pleased with and write the recipe that produced it.
Generate three more subjects using the same recipe unchanged.
Put all four side by side and look for the drift.
Tighten whichever specification drifted, then repeat.

blocks.heading: Sell the Recipe Too
blocks.bodyHtml:
The recipe is a deliverable. Handing over a documented style — with the exact specifications — is something clients value and few freelancers offer.

It does not cost you future work. It usually creates it, because the client now has a standard they want maintained, and maintaining it is a monthly job.

blocks.body: Clients can make one good image themselves; they cannot make forty that match. Fix the palette, light, framing and realism as a written recipe, build it once and vary only the subject. Hand the recipe over as a deliverable — it creates maintenance work rather than removing it.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: delivering files a client can actually use without coming back to you.

lessons.title: Delivering Files a Client Can Use

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Visual work has a delivery problem that writing does not. The images can be exactly right and the job still feels unfinished, because the client cannot get them into the places they need to go.

This is where a lot of goodwill quietly disappears — not in the work, but in the twenty minutes afterwards when they discover the file is the wrong shape.

blocks.heading: Ask Where It Will Live
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every destination has its own requirements, and the client will not think to mention them.

«Here are the twenty images.»

«Twenty images, each in three crops: square for the shop, wide for the site banner, tall for stories. Named by product code.»

The second version is the difference between files and a finished job.

blocks.text: A file the client has to resize themselves is a job that is not finished.

blocks.heading: Four Things That Make Files Usable
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Named systematically — product code, not «final_v3_new».
  • Right sizes — the crops each destination actually needs
  • Right weight — compressed for web, so pages stay fast
  • One folder — a single link, organised, nothing to hunt for

None of this is creative work. All of it is what makes the client describe you as easy to work with, which is what gets repeated.

blocks.question: You deliver twenty images and the client asks for them all in a different size. What went wrong?

options.label: Nothing — resizing requests are a normal part of any visual project.
You did not ask where the images would be used before producing them.
You generated at too low a resolution to allow easy resizing later.
The client changed their mind about the platforms after seeing the work.

blocks.successBody: Destinations decide dimensions, and the client rarely volunteers them. One question at the briefing stage — where will these appear — prevents an entire round of rework at the end.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which question at the start would have made this request unnecessary.

blocks.heading: Say What They May Do With It
blocks.bodyHtml:
Include one line on usage: what they can use the images for, and whether anything is restricted.

Rules around generated imagery vary by tool and change over time. Being the freelancer who mentioned it, rather than the one who was asked afterwards, is a small thing that reads as professional and prevents an awkward conversation later.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write the question you will ask about destinations in every visual brief.
Build your standard folder structure and naming convention now.
Export one image in the three most common crops you deliver.
Draft your one-line usage note so it never has to be improvised.

blocks.heading: Keep the Originals
blocks.bodyHtml:
Keep full-resolution versions and the recipe that produced them for at least a year, organised by client.

Requests come back months later — a new size, one more product in the same style. Being able to answer in ten minutes rather than rebuilding from nothing is worth the storage many times over.

blocks.body: Visual jobs are finished at the file, not at the image. Ask where they will appear, deliver the crops each destination needs, name files systematically, compress for the web and send one organised link. Add a line about usage rights, and keep originals and recipes for a year.

modules.title: Brand Kits As a Service
modules.description: Package visual identity work into a fixed-price product. Covers what goes in a kit, how to present it, and how to keep revisions from eating the fee.

lessons.title: What Actually Goes in a Brand Kit

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Small businesses rarely want a brand strategy. They want to stop making the same five decisions every time they post something, and to look like one company rather than several.

A brand kit is the answer to that, and it is one of the easiest things to sell as a fixed-price product — provided you build the version people actually use.

blocks.heading: Small and Used Beats Complete and Ignored
blocks.bodyHtml:
The instinct is to make it thorough, because thorough looks like value.

A forty-page document covering values, personality, tone and extensive usage rules.

Two pages: the colours as values, two fonts with sizes, three logo files, and five example posts.

The second gets opened on a phone before a post goes out. The first gets saved and never read again.

blocks.text: A brand kit nobody opens on a phone is a document, not a tool.

blocks.heading: The Six Things Worth Including
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Colours — as copyable values, with what each is for
  • Two fonts — heading and body, with actual sizes
  • Logo files — light, dark, and a small square version
  • Image style — three examples of right, one of wrong
  • Five templates — the formats they post most
  • One page of rules — the decisions, nothing else

Six items, deliverable in a few days, and each one removes a recurring decision.

blocks.question: A small shop wants «branding». What is the most useful first deliverable?

options.label: A brand strategy document covering values, positioning and personality.
Two pages of colours, fonts, logos and five ready-to-use templates.
A new logo, since that is the foundation everything else builds on.
A competitor analysis showing how similar shops present themselves.

blocks.successBody: What a small shop needs is to stop making the same decisions weekly. Colours, fonts and templates do that immediately, while strategy documents and competitor analyses change nothing about tomorrow's post.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which deliverable changes what happens the very next time they post something.

blocks.heading: Templates Are the Real Product
blocks.bodyHtml:
The rules page is what you write; the templates are what they use. Five editable templates in whatever tool they already have will be opened weekly for years.

Build them in the tool the client actually uses, not the one you prefer. A template they cannot edit is a picture of a template, and it teaches them that the kit does not fit how they work.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick a small business and list the five things they post most often.
Build one template for the most frequent format.
Write the one-page rules — decisions only, no explanation of theory.
Check the whole kit is readable on a phone screen.

blocks.heading: Show the Wrong Version
blocks.bodyHtml:
Include one example of what not to do — the stretched logo, the off-palette colour, the wrong photo style.

People learn boundaries much faster from a wrong example than from a rule, and this single page prevents most of the drift that otherwise appears within a few months.

blocks.body: Small businesses want fewer decisions, not a strategy. Deliver two pages: colours as copyable values, two fonts with sizes, three logo files, an image style with examples, five editable templates in their own tool, and one page of rules including one wrong example.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: presenting the kit so it gets used rather than filed.

lessons.title: Presenting It So It Gets Used

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
A kit that is never opened produces no visible change, and a client who sees no change does not commission anything else. The presentation is not decoration — it is what determines whether the work has any effect.

Most of it comes down to reducing the number of steps between the client and the decision they need to make.

blocks.heading: Deliver Where They Work
blocks.bodyHtml:
Format decides usage more than content does.

A polished PDF sent as an email attachment.

A shared folder with the templates already inside the tool they use, plus a two-page summary they can open on a phone.

The PDF looks more like a deliverable. The folder is the one that changes what they post next week.

blocks.text: Every step between the client and the decision is a chance for the kit to go unused.

blocks.heading: Walk Them Through It Once
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Fifteen minutes, screen shared or recorded
  • Make one real post with them, using a template
  • Show the wrong example and why it is wrong
  • Leave the recording for whoever joins the business later

That recording keeps working long after you have gone, and it is often what makes the kit survive a change of staff.

blocks.question: Two months after delivery, the client's posts look inconsistent again. What most likely went wrong?

options.label: The kit itself was not detailed enough to cover all their situations.
It was never made part of how they actually create posts each week.
They hired someone new who has different taste in visual design.
The templates were too restrictive for the content they wanted to post.

blocks.successBody: Kits fail at adoption far more often than at design. If the templates are not inside the tool they open every week, the old habits win by default — regardless of how good the rules were.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about where the kit lives compared to where the work actually happens.

blocks.heading: Check Back at Thirty Days
blocks.bodyHtml:
Send one message a month later: «How are the templates working? Anything you keep needing that isn't there?»

It costs a sentence and produces two things — small paid additions, and the knowledge of what a kit should include next time. It is also the most natural possible opening for further work.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Decide where your kits will live — the tool, not the file format.
Write your fifteen-minute walkthrough outline.
Draft the thirty-day check-in message now.
Add a line to your delivery offering to make the first post together.

blocks.heading: Name the Owner
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ask who inside the business will actually use this, and address the kit to that person rather than to the owner who commissioned it.

Very often those are different people, and the kit that was handed to a director never reaches whoever posts on Thursday. Sending it to both, with a note, takes ten seconds and doubles the chance it gets used.

blocks.body: Kits fail at adoption, not design. Deliver into the tool they already use, walk them through it once and record it, make one real post together, then check back at thirty days. Ask who will actually use it and address it to that person, not only to whoever paid.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: pricing kits so revisions do not consume the fee.

lessons.title: Fixed Price, Fixed Revisions

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Visual work attracts opinions in a way that written work does not. Everyone has a view on a colour, and every view arrives as a small request.

This is why unbounded revision is far more dangerous here than anywhere else. The work is never wrong exactly — it is just not quite what someone pictured, and that can continue indefinitely.

blocks.heading: Rounds, Not Requests
blocks.bodyHtml:
The structure of feedback matters more than the number of changes.

«Let me know any changes you'd like and I'll adjust them.»

«Two rounds included. Please collect all comments from everyone into one message per round.»

The second prevents the worst pattern in visual work: three people sending contradictory notes over five days, each expecting a new version.

blocks.text: Unlimited revisions do not make clients happier. They make decisions optional.

blocks.heading: Present Options Once, Then Refine
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Round one — two or three directions, deliberately different
  • They pick one — a decision, in writing
  • Round two — refinement of the chosen one only
  • Delivery — files, templates, walkthrough

Presenting three directions and then refining one is far quicker than showing a single option and adjusting it until it becomes something else.

blocks.question: After choosing a direction, the client asks to see the rejected option «one more time, adjusted». What now?

options.label: Show it — it costs little and keeping them happy matters more here.
Note it is a new direction, and offer it as a priced extra round.
Refuse and remind them they already made a decision in writing.
Combine both directions into one version to satisfy everyone involved.

blocks.successBody: Reopening a rejected direction is new work, not a revision. Naming it and pricing it keeps the project finite, while quietly absorbing it teaches the client that decisions can always be reversed for free.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask whether this request is refining the chosen work or restarting the choice.

blocks.heading: Ask Who Approves Before Starting
blocks.bodyHtml:
The most expensive question in visual work is the one asked too late: who has final say?

If a partner, a spouse or a marketing lead has to be happy, get them into round one. Discovering a second decision-maker at the end means starting again, usually for free.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your revision policy in one sentence, including consolidated feedback.
Add the approval question to your standard briefing message.
Decide your price for an extra round and write it down now.
Draft the polite line you use when a request reopens a decision.

blocks.heading: Get the Choice in Writing
blocks.bodyHtml:
When they pick a direction, confirm it in a message: «Going with direction B — refining that one now.»

It sounds excessive for a friendly project and it is the thing that makes the conversation above possible. Without it, the disagreement is about memory, and memory conveniently favours whoever is paying.

blocks.body: Visual work invites endless small opinions, so structure the feedback: two rounds, consolidated comments, three directions first and refinement of one afterwards. Confirm the chosen direction in writing, ask who approves before starting, and price reopened decisions as new work.

modules.title: Automation Without Code
modules.description: Sell time back to a business by connecting the tools it already pays for. Covers mapping a manual process, building it, and proving the hours saved.

lessons.title: Find the Hour That Repeats

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Automation is usually sold as a technology decision — which tools connect to which. That framing is why most automation projects go nowhere: nobody could say what they were for.

The useful version starts somewhere else entirely. Find one hour a week that a person spends doing the same thing, and the project has a purpose, a price and a way to prove it worked.

blocks.heading: Ask About the Week, Not the Systems
blocks.bodyHtml:
The discovery question decides the whole job.

«Which tools do you use, and what would you like to automate?»

«What did someone do three times this week that was exactly the same each time?»

The first invites a wish list nobody can price. The second produces a real task, with a real person attached, and usually a real number of hours.

blocks.text: Nobody buys automation. They buy an hour back, every week, forever.

blocks.heading: What Makes a Task Automatable
blocks.bodyHtml:
• It repeats — weekly at least, ideally daily
  • The rules are stable — the same input leads to the same decision
  • The data is already digital — in a form, a sheet, an inbox
  • A mistake is recoverable — nothing irreversible on the first build

Fail the second and you are automating a judgement, which needs a human check in the middle. Fail the fourth and you should not be the person building it yet.

blocks.question: Which task is the best first automation project for a small business?

options.label: Deciding which customers should receive a refund and how much to give.
Copying form entries into a sheet and sending the team a daily summary.
Writing personalised replies to every incoming customer complaint.
Choosing which products to discount based on this month's stock levels.

blocks.successBody: Copying and summarising is repetitive, rule-based, already digital and harmless if it breaks. The other three all involve judgement with money or relationships attached, which is where a first build should not be.
blocks.wrongHint: Look for the task where the same input always leads to the same correct action.

blocks.heading: Count the Hours Out Loud
blocks.bodyHtml:
Before building anything, agree the number: «this takes about forty minutes, three times a week». Write it in the message.

That number is what you are selling, what justifies your price, and what you will point at in a month. Skipping it is why so many automation jobs end with a client vaguely wondering whether it was worth it.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Ask one business owner what they did three times this week identically.
Write the task as: trigger, steps, result — no tools mentioned yet.
Estimate the minutes it takes and how often it happens.
Check it against the four conditions above before offering anything.

blocks.heading: Start Smaller Than You Want To
blocks.bodyHtml:
The temptation with a first automation client is to redesign their whole process, because you can see how much is wrong with it.

Automate one step instead. A small thing that works on Monday buys you the trust to look at the rest — and a large thing that half-works teaches them that automation is unreliable, which closes the door for everyone.

blocks.body: Automation projects fail when they start from tools. Start from one repeating hour: ask what someone did three times identically this week, check it is rule-based, digital and safe to get wrong, then agree the number of minutes it costs today. Automate one step, not the whole process.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: building it so it survives the week you are not watching.

lessons.title: Build It Once, Then Prove It Works

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Getting an automation to run once is the easy part, and it is where beginners declare victory. The client sees a demonstration, everyone is pleased, and the handover happens.

Then something arrives in a format nobody anticipated, the flow fails silently, and three weeks later the client is back to doing it by hand — without telling you.

blocks.heading: Build for the Odd Case
blocks.bodyHtml:
The difference between a demo and a service is what happens when the input is wrong.

A flow that works perfectly on the five test entries you made yourself.

A flow that handles a blank field, a duplicate, an unexpected format — and tells someone when it cannot.

Real data is messier than test data, always. The odd case is not an edge case; it is Tuesday.

blocks.text: A flow that fails silently is worse than no flow, because now nobody is checking.

blocks.heading: Four Things Every Build Needs
blocks.bodyHtml:
• A failure alert — a message to a real person when it breaks
  • A log — what ran, when, and what it did
  • A manual override — a way to run or skip it by hand
  • A test with real data — theirs, not yours, before it goes live

These four take an extra hour and are the difference between something still running in six months and something quietly abandoned in three weeks.

blocks.question: Your automation ran fine for two weeks, then stopped without anyone noticing. What was missing?

options.label: More thorough testing of every possible input before it went live.
An alert to a named person the moment a run fails to complete.
Better documentation explaining how the whole flow was constructed.
A more reliable set of tools with fewer connections between them.

blocks.successBody: Everything breaks eventually — that is not the failure. The failure is that nobody found out. An alert to a named person turns an invisible outage into a fifteen-minute fix.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which answer addresses «without anyone noticing» rather than «stopped».

blocks.heading: Prove It With Their Numbers
blocks.bodyHtml:
Two weeks after launch, send one line: «It has run 34 times, handled 210 entries, and failed twice — both fixed. That is roughly six hours not spent.»

This is the single most valuable message in the whole project. It converts an invisible background process into a visible result, and it is what makes the next automation an easy conversation.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any flow you have built and list what happens if the input is blank.
Add a failure alert that reaches a person, not a log nobody opens.
Run it on real data with the client watching, not on your own samples.
Write the two-week proof message before you even launch it.

blocks.heading: Hand Over More Than Access
blocks.bodyHtml:
Give the client a one-page note: what it does, what triggers it, who gets alerts, how to pause it, and what to do if it breaks.

Freelancers often keep this vague, believing it protects future work. It does the opposite — a client who feels trapped by a system they cannot understand does not commission a second one.

blocks.body: A demo becomes a service when it survives bad input. Add a failure alert, a log, a manual override, and a test on real data. Two weeks later, send the numbers — runs, items handled, hours saved. Hand over a one-page note so nobody feels trapped by what you built.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: pricing something that keeps working after you have left.

lessons.title: Price the Time Saved, Not the Tools

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Automation is the work where hourly billing is most obviously wrong. A flow that takes you three hours to build can save a business four hours every week for years.

Bill for your three hours and you have priced your typing speed. The client received something worth two hundred hours a year, and neither of you noticed what just happened.

blocks.heading: Anchor on Their Number
blocks.bodyHtml:
You already agreed the hours in the first conversation. Use them.

«It took me about four hours, so £160.»

«This replaces about two hours a week. £450 to build, and you're ahead within a couple of months.»

The second is judged against what it saves, which is the only number that has anything to do with what it is worth.

blocks.text: Bill for your build hours and you have priced your typing speed, not the result.

blocks.heading: Three Parts to Charge For
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The build — one fee, anchored on the time it replaces
  • The care — a small monthly amount for monitoring and fixes
  • The changes — new steps or new cases, priced as small add-ons

Most freelancers charge only for the first and then do the other two free, which is exactly how automation becomes an unpaid support job.

blocks.question: Your flow took three hours to build and saves the client three hours every week. How do you price it?

options.label: Three hours at your usual hourly rate, since that is what it took you.
A build fee anchored on the weekly saving, plus a small monthly care fee.
A percentage of the money the business saves, calculated every quarter.
Nothing up front, with a larger monthly fee for as long as it keeps running.

blocks.successBody: A build fee based on what it replaces captures the value, and a small care fee funds the maintenance that will definitely be needed. Percentage deals require accounting nobody wants, and no build fee leaves you exposed if they cancel early.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which structure pays for both the value created and the work that comes later.

blocks.heading: Charge Something for Care
blocks.bodyHtml:
Tools change, formats shift, connections expire. Something will need attention within a few months — this is normal, not a defect.

A small monthly fee makes that expected and paid. Without it, every fix is an awkward favour, and you end up either resenting the client or ignoring the message.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a flow idea and write what it would save per week, in minutes.
Set a build fee anchored on that, not on your build time.
Add a monthly care fee and say exactly what it covers.
Write the sentence explaining why care is not optional, in plain words.

blocks.heading: The Second One Is Easier
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once a business has seen one process get quieter, they start noticing the others themselves. The second project usually needs no selling at all.

This is why the two-week proof message matters so much. It is not a report — it is the thing that makes someone look around their own week and find the next hour to hand you.

blocks.body: Automation is worth what it replaces, not what it costs you to build. Anchor the fee on the hours saved, add a small monthly care fee so maintenance is expected and paid, and price changes as add-ons. Then prove the saving — that is what produces the second project.

modules.title: AI Assistants As a Service
modules.description: Build a working assistant for one specific job a client does every week. Covers scoping, guardrails, handover, and pricing something that keeps running.

lessons.title: An Assistant Is a Job Description

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Businesses now ask for «an AI assistant» the way they used to ask for «a website» — as a thing they have heard about, without a clear picture of what it does.

Delivered as a general helper, it gets used twice and abandoned. The ones that stay in use are the ones built for a single named job, and that difference is decided before any building starts.

blocks.heading: Narrow Beats Clever
blocks.bodyHtml:
Compare two versions of the same project:

«An assistant that helps the team with customer questions.»

«Answers the eleven questions we get about delivery, using our real policy, and hands anything else to a person.»

The second can be tested, corrected and trusted. The first cannot even be judged — there is no standard to hold it to.

blocks.text: An assistant that could do anything gets used for nothing.

blocks.heading: Write It Like a Job Ad
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The tasks — listed, countable, nothing vague
  • The sources — exactly which documents it may use
  • The limits — what it must never answer or promise
  • The escalation — who it hands to, and when

If you would not hire a person on this description, the assistant is not defined well enough to build yet. Writing this document is most of the actual work.

blocks.question: A client asks for «an AI assistant for the business». What do you deliver first?

options.label: A general assistant trained on all their documents that anyone can query.
A one-page description of the single job it will do, agreed before building.
A demonstration of what the technology can do, to spark ideas for later.
A comparison of the available tools with a recommendation on which to use.

blocks.successBody: The scoping document is the deliverable that makes everything else possible, and clients will pay for it. Building before the job is defined produces something nobody can evaluate and nobody ends up using.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what has to exist before you could tell whether the finished thing is any good.

blocks.heading: Sell the Definition Separately
blocks.bodyHtml:
That one-page description is a paid first stage. It takes a couple of hours, produces something genuinely useful even if they stop there, and it protects you from building against a moving target.

It also filters. A client who will not pay for two hours of definition was not going to be a good client for the twenty hours that follow.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick a business you know and name one job an assistant could do there.
Write the four sections: tasks, sources, limits, escalation.
Read it as a job ad — would you hire someone on this description?
Note every place you had to guess; those are the questions to ask the client.

blocks.heading: Count the Questions First
blocks.bodyHtml:
Before agreeing to anything, ask for real examples — the last fifty enquiries, the actual questions people ask.

You will usually find that a handful of questions cover most of the volume. That is the scope of the first version, and it makes a genuinely difficult project into a small, finishable one.

blocks.body: Assistants fail when they are general. Define one job as if writing a job ad — tasks, permitted sources, hard limits, escalation — and sell that definition as a paid first stage. Look at fifty real enquiries first: a handful of questions usually cover most of the volume.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: the guardrails that have to exist before capability.

lessons.title: Guardrails Before Capability

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The interesting part of building an assistant is making it capable. The part that decides whether it survives contact with real customers is making it refuse.

One confidently wrong answer about a refund, a price or a legal question costs more than a hundred correct ones earned. That asymmetry should shape the whole build.

blocks.heading: Design the Refusals First
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most builds start with what it should do and add limits at the end, if at all.

«It answers customer questions using our documents.»

«It never quotes a price, never promises a delivery date, never discusses refunds — those three always go to a person.»

Writing the refusals first makes them explicit and testable, rather than something you hope the model works out.

blocks.text: One confidently wrong answer about money undoes a hundred correct ones.

blocks.heading: Four Guardrails Worth Having
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Source limits — it answers only from approved documents
  • Topic bans — money, legal, medical, anything binding
  • Uncertainty behaviour — say «I'll pass this on» rather than guess
  • A visible label — people are told they are talking to a tool

The third is the one everybody forgets, and it is the one that prevents the situation you would least like to explain to a client.

blocks.question: During testing the assistant invents a delivery time that is not in the documents. What is the fix?

options.label: Add more documents so it has the correct delivery information available.
Ban the topic outright and route every delivery question to a person.
Instruct it to be more careful and accurate when discussing delivery.
Accept it as a rare edge case that customers are unlikely to trigger.

blocks.successBody: Anything the business would be held to — dates, prices, promises — should be a hard route to a human rather than a matter of instruction quality. Asking a model to be careful is a preference; a topic ban is a rule.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which fix still holds when the model behaves unpredictably next month.

blocks.heading: Test With Hostile Input
blocks.bodyHtml:
Before launch, spend an hour trying to break it: confusing phrasing, questions outside scope, requests to ignore its instructions, angry customers.

Do this with the client watching. It builds enormous trust, it surfaces the real limits, and it means both of you agreed what the boundaries were before anyone else found them.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write the three topics your assistant will always refuse.
Write its exact wording for «I do not know» — it should be one friendly line.
Spend twenty minutes trying to make a test assistant say something wrong.
Record what worked; those become test cases before every change.

blocks.heading: Say What It Is
blocks.bodyHtml:
People should know they are talking to a tool, and should always have a visible way to reach a person.

Beyond the obvious fairness, it is practical: expectations drop to something reasonable, and a customer who knows they can escalate does not spend four messages getting angry at software.

blocks.body: Build the refusals before the capabilities: approved sources only, hard bans on anything binding, a clear «I'll pass this on» for uncertainty, and a visible label. Test with hostile input while the client watches, so the limits are agreed before a customer finds them.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: handing it over so it is still running in six months.

lessons.title: Handover, and What Happens After

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
An assistant is not a file you deliver. It is something that keeps running, on live inputs, in a business that changes — which makes handover a different problem from any other freelance delivery.

Handled badly, it becomes either an abandoned experiment or an unpaid support role. Handled well, it is the most reliable recurring income in this whole field.

blocks.heading: Launch Quietly
blocks.bodyHtml:
Do not switch it on for every customer on day one.

Full launch, all channels, the moment testing looks good.

Two weeks answering internally, or drafting replies a person approves before sending.

A soft launch surfaces the real questions — which are never the ones you predicted — while mistakes are still private and cheap.

blocks.text: The questions real customers ask are never the ones you tested for.

blocks.heading: What the Client Must Be Able to Do Alone
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Turn it off — one obvious control, no message to you required
  • See what it said — a log a non-technical person can read
  • Add a fact — update a source document without your involvement
  • Reach you — a clear route when something is actually wrong

Withholding the first three does not protect your income. It makes the client nervous, and nervous clients quietly stop using things.

blocks.question: How should an assistant that answers customers be launched?

options.label: Fully live once testing passes, with monitoring for the first busy week.
Drafting replies for a person to approve first, then live after two weeks.
Live only outside working hours at first, when the volume is much lower.
Live for a small random share of customers, increasing gradually each week.

blocks.successBody: Human-approved drafts surface every real question while every mistake stays internal. It also produces a fortnight of corrections that make the live version genuinely good rather than merely tested.
blocks.wrongHint: Look for the option where real questions are discovered before any customer sees an answer.

blocks.heading: Review Monthly, Charge for It
blocks.bodyHtml:
Sell a monthly review: read a sample of conversations, fix the misses, add new facts, report what customers are actually asking.

That last part is worth more than the assistant. A monthly summary of real customer questions is business intelligence the client has never had, and it makes the retainer obviously worth keeping.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your soft-launch plan: how long, who approves, what you measure.
List the four controls the client must have and check each exists.
Draft the one-page operating note in plain language, no jargon.
Write what your monthly review covers and what it costs.

blocks.heading: Plan for the Day It Is Wrong
blocks.bodyHtml:
At some point it will say something incorrect to a real customer. Agree in advance who is told, how quickly it is corrected, and who speaks to the customer.

Having that conversation before launch turns an alarming incident into a procedure. Having it afterwards, under pressure, is how a good project ends badly.

blocks.body: Launch softly with human-approved drafts, then live. Give the client four controls they can use alone: off, logs, adding facts, reaching you. Sell a monthly review — the summary of what customers actually ask is worth more than the assistant — and agree the incident procedure before launch.

modules.title: Data Work With AI
modules.description: Turn messy spreadsheets into answers a business can act on. Covers cleaning, summarising, and checking AI output before it reaches a client.

lessons.title: Cleaning Is Most of the Job

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Data work sounds like analysis: find the insight, spot the trend, explain what it means. That is the part everybody wants to talk about, and it is maybe a fifth of the time.

The rest is making the data trustworthy enough to analyse. Skip it and you will produce a confident answer built on duplicated rows and three different spellings of the same city.

blocks.heading: Real Data Is Always Messy
blocks.bodyHtml:
Client spreadsheets are not databases. They are the record of many people typing things over several years.

Loading the file and asking for the top-selling products straight away.

Checking first: duplicate rows, inconsistent dates, blank fields, three spellings of one supplier, refunds counted as sales.

Every one of those changes the answer. None of them announces itself.

blocks.text: An answer from dirty data is not a rough answer. It is a wrong one delivered confidently.

blocks.heading: Five Checks Before Any Analysis
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Row count — does it match what the client expects?
  • Date range — is the period what you think it is?
  • Duplicates — same order counted twice?
  • Categories — how many spellings of the same thing?
  • Blanks — which columns have gaps, and how many?

Ten minutes of checking. It also gives you the first thing worth telling the client, often before you have analysed anything.

blocks.question: A client's sales file gives a total 12% higher than their accounts. What do you do first?

options.label: Report the higher figure, since the raw data is the more reliable source.
Find the discrepancy — likely duplicates, refunds or an overlapping period.
Adjust the total downwards by 12% so it matches the official accounts.
Report both numbers and let the client decide which one to rely on.

blocks.successBody: A gap between two sources is information, not noise. Finding its cause usually reveals a real problem in how the data is recorded — which is often more valuable to the client than the analysis they asked for.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which response treats the discrepancy as something to explain rather than something to smooth over.

blocks.heading: AI Helps, But Verify the Method
blocks.bodyHtml:
AI is genuinely good at the tedious parts: spotting inconsistent formats, suggesting how to normalise categories, writing the transformation steps.

What it should not do unchecked is decide what counts. Whether a refund is a negative sale or an excluded row is a business decision — ask the client, then apply it consistently and say so in the output.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Find any public spreadsheet and run the five checks on it.
Count how many spellings exist for the categories in one column.
Write down every decision you had to make to clean it.
Note which of those decisions a client should really have made.

blocks.heading: Show Your Cleaning
blocks.bodyHtml:
Include a short note with any analysis: rows removed, duplicates found, assumptions made, what was excluded and why.

Clients almost never ask for this, and it is the thing that makes the numbers defensible when someone internally disagrees with them. It also quietly proves the work was more than pasting a file into a tool.

blocks.body: Most data work is making the data trustworthy. Run five checks before analysing — row count, date range, duplicates, category spellings, blanks — and let the client make the business decisions about what counts. Then show your cleaning, so the numbers can be defended.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: why you should never deliver a number you cannot verify by hand.

lessons.title: Never Ship a Number You Cannot Check

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The most dangerous thing about generated analysis is how convincing it looks. A clean table with plausible figures reads as authoritative regardless of whether the calculation was right.

In writing, a weak draft is obvious. In data, a wrong answer looks exactly like a correct one — and the client may act on it before anyone notices.

blocks.heading: Check One Row by Hand
blocks.bodyHtml:
The habit that prevents most of these failures takes two minutes.

Accepting the summary table because the numbers look reasonable.

Picking one product, adding its sales manually, and confirming the total matches the table.

If one row is right, the method is probably right. If it is wrong, you have just avoided delivering a report built on a broken calculation.

blocks.text: A wrong number looks exactly like a right one. That is what makes data work risky.

blocks.heading: Four Things Worth Verifying
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Totals — do the parts add to the whole?
  • One row by hand — recalculate a single case yourself
  • Extremes — is the biggest value plausible, or a data error?
  • Direction — does the trend match what the client already knows?

The last one catches the most. Clients know their own business, and «that doesn't sound right» is usually correct.

blocks.question: Your analysis shows one product accounts for 60% of revenue. The client is surprised. What now?

options.label: Present it as a genuine finding — surprising results are often the valuable ones.
Verify that product's rows by hand before presenting the number at all.
Soften it by describing the product as one of the stronger performers.
Exclude it as an outlier and report the pattern across the other products.

blocks.successBody: Surprise from someone who knows the business is a signal to check, not to celebrate or to hide. Often it is a duplicated import or a bundle counted individually — and finding that is worth more than the original analysis.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what the client's surprise is telling you about the data rather than about the business.

blocks.heading: Say What You Are Not Sure About
blocks.bodyHtml:
Uncertainty stated plainly reads as competence: «This assumes refunds are excluded — if they are included, the top three change order.»

Clients make better decisions with that sentence than without it, and it protects you when a number is later questioned. Presenting everything with equal confidence is what damages trust the first time something turns out to be wrong.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any generated summary of a dataset and recalculate one row by hand.
Check whether the parts actually add up to the stated total.
Look at the largest value and ask whether it is plausible.
Write one sentence naming the biggest assumption in the analysis.

blocks.heading: Keep the Steps
blocks.bodyHtml:
Save the sequence you used to get from raw file to answer — the transformations, in order.

Two things follow: you can rerun it next month in minutes instead of hours, and when someone asks how a figure was produced, you can show them. That combination is what turns one-off analysis into a monthly retainer.

blocks.body: Wrong numbers look identical to right ones, so verify before delivering: check totals, recalculate one row by hand, sanity-check extremes, and test the direction against what the client already knows. State assumptions plainly and keep your steps so the work can be repeated and defended.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: turning a verified spreadsheet into a decision someone can actually make.

lessons.title: Turning a Spreadsheet Into a Decision

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
A correct analysis that changes nothing is a failed job, even when every number is right. This is the most common way data work disappoints — it answers the question asked rather than the decision behind it.

Clients ask for analysis because something needs deciding. Finding out what that is turns a spreadsheet into work worth paying for again.

blocks.heading: Ask What They Will Do With It
blocks.bodyHtml:
One question at the briefing stage changes the entire deliverable.

«You'd like a breakdown of sales by product and month — I'll send that over.»

«What are you deciding? Whether to drop products, where to spend the ad budget, or what to stock next season?»

Each of those three answers produces a completely different analysis of the same file.

blocks.text: Nobody wants a breakdown. They want to know what to do on Monday.

blocks.heading: Answer in This Order
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The answer — one sentence, first, before any method
  • The evidence — the two or three numbers that support it
  • The caveat — what would change the answer
  • The next step — what you would do, concretely

Reports written the other way round — method, tables, then conclusion — are read to the end by almost nobody, including the person who commissioned them.

blocks.question: A client asks for «an analysis of last year's sales». What is the most useful first response?

options.label: Deliver a full breakdown by product, month, region and customer type.
Ask what decision this is feeding, then analyse for that specific question.
Ask which chart types and format they would like the report delivered in.
Analyse everything you can find and highlight whatever looks interesting.

blocks.successBody: The same data supports completely different analyses depending on the decision behind the request. Asking takes one message and is the difference between a report that is read and one that is filed.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which response changes what you actually produce rather than how it looks.

blocks.heading: Cut Everything That Is Merely Interesting
blocks.bodyHtml:
You will find patterns unrelated to the decision. It is tempting to include them, because they show effort and they are genuinely interesting to you.

Put them in one short «also noticed» line at the end, or save them for the next conversation. Mixed into the main answer, they dilute it — and the client stops being able to tell what you are recommending.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any dataset and write the decision it might inform, in one sentence.
Produce the answer to that decision in a single sentence, before any charts.
Add the two numbers that support it and the one caveat that could change it.
Check whether anything else you found actually belongs in the report.

blocks.heading: Say What You Would Do
blocks.bodyHtml:
Clients often want a recommendation and are reluctant to ask for one, because it feels like admitting they cannot read their own data.

Offer it plainly: «If it were mine, I'd stop stocking the bottom four and put that budget into the top two.» You may be overruled, and you will still be the person who is thinking about the business rather than the file.

blocks.body: Analysis that changes nothing is a failed job. Ask what decision the work feeds, answer in one sentence before any method, then evidence, caveat and next step. Keep merely interesting findings out of the main answer, and say plainly what you would do.

modules.title: Reports Clients Act On
modules.description: Deliver findings people read instead of file away. Covers structure, one-chart-one-point, and the recommendation that turns a report into more work.

lessons.title: Why Reports Get Filed Unread

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most reports are thorough, accurate and unread. The freelancer who made one usually concludes the client is not interested in detail, which is the wrong lesson.

The client is interested. They just could not find, in the time they had, what the report wanted them to do — and a document that requires an hour to yield a decision gets postponed until it is stale.

blocks.heading: Front-Load the Conclusion
blocks.bodyHtml:
Reports are usually built like an argument: context, method, findings, conclusion. That order is exactly backwards for a busy reader.

Twelve pages building carefully towards a recommendation on page eleven.

One page: here is what we found, here is what to do, here is what it rests on. Detail behind it for anyone who wants it.

Nobody has ever complained that the conclusion came too early.

blocks.text: A report that takes an hour to yield a decision will be read next month, when it no longer matters.

blocks.heading: Four Reasons Reports Fail
blocks.bodyHtml:
• No single answer — findings listed, nothing concluded
  • Too many charts — twelve visuals, no argument
  • No recommendation — data handed over, decision left open
  • Wrong audience — written for an analyst, read by an owner

Each is a formatting failure rather than an analysis failure, which is good news: they are all fixable in twenty minutes.

blocks.question: A client says your last report was «very thorough» but nothing changed afterwards. What went wrong?

options.label: The analysis was not deep enough to reveal anything genuinely actionable.
It presented findings without a single clear answer and recommended action.
The client is not the kind of person who makes decisions from data.
The report should have included more charts to make the patterns clearer.

blocks.successBody: «Very thorough» with no action is the classic signal that the reader could not find the point. Findings without a conclusion put the interpretation back on the busiest person, and it does not get done.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what «thorough but nothing changed» actually tells you about the reader's experience.

blocks.heading: Write for the Person Who Decides
blocks.bodyHtml:
Before writing, ask who will read this and what they know. An owner needs plain language and consequences; a specialist wants method and caveats.

Writing at the wrong level is not a small mistake — it makes the whole document feel either patronising or impenetrable, and both get filed.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any report you have seen and find its main conclusion.
Note how far down the page it appears.
Rewrite the first three lines so the answer comes first.
Cut any chart that does not support that answer directly.

blocks.heading: One Page, Then Everything Else
blocks.bodyHtml:
Structure every report the same way: one page that stands alone, then the detail behind it.

The one page is what gets read, forwarded and acted on. The detail exists so that when someone challenges a number, the answer is available — and that is exactly what it should be for.

blocks.body: Reports fail on format, not analysis. Put the conclusion first, write for the person deciding rather than for a specialist, and make page one stand alone with the detail behind it. «Very thorough, nothing changed» means the reader could not find the point.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: making each chart carry exactly one idea.

lessons.title: One Chart, One Point

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Charts are the most misused part of a report. They get added because a page of text looks bare, not because there is something a picture explains better than a sentence.

The result is a document that looks analytical and communicates less than three plain lines would have — and takes longer to read.

blocks.heading: Every Chart Needs a Sentence
blocks.bodyHtml:
The fastest test: can you write the point of the chart in one sentence? If not, the chart does not have a point yet.

A chart titled «Monthly revenue by category, 2025».

The same chart titled «Two categories carry the year — everything else is flat».

The first labels the data. The second tells the reader what to see, which is the entire job of the visual.

blocks.text: If you cannot write the chart's point in one sentence, the chart has no point yet.

blocks.heading: Rules That Make Charts Readable
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Title states the finding, not the axes
  • One idea per chart — two ideas means two charts
  • Highlight the point — one colour, everything else grey
  • Order by size, not alphabetically, unless time is the axis
  • Label directly — a legend is one more lookup

These take a minute each and are the difference between a chart that is understood at a glance and one that is skipped.

blocks.question: You want to show that one product outsells all others. What is the clearest chart?

options.label: A pie chart showing every product's share of total sales for the year.
A bar chart sorted by size with that one product in a stronger colour.
A line chart of monthly sales for each product across the whole year.
A table of all products with their totals and percentages listed.

blocks.successBody: Sorted bars make comparison immediate, and colouring only the subject tells the eye where to look. Pie charts hide differences between similar slices, and multi-line charts bury one product among many.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option makes the comparison obvious without the reader doing any work.

blocks.heading: Fewer Charts, Better Ones
blocks.bodyHtml:
Three charts that each carry a point beat twelve that catalogue the data. Every additional chart divides the reader's attention and dilutes the argument.

A good rule when finishing a report: remove the weakest chart and check whether anything is lost. Usually nothing is, and the report gets stronger.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any chart and rewrite its title as the finding it shows.
Grey out everything except the part that supports the point.
Sort the categories by size and see whether it reads faster.
Remove one chart from a report and check what is actually lost.

blocks.heading: Numbers in Sentences Are Fine
blocks.bodyHtml:
Not everything needs a visual. «Three products make 62% of revenue» is clearer as a sentence than as any chart.

Use charts for comparison, distribution and change over time. For a single striking number, write the number — it is faster to read and impossible to misinterpret.

blocks.body: A chart earns its place only if you can state its point in one sentence. Title with the finding, keep one idea per chart, highlight the subject and grey the rest, sort by size and label directly. Three purposeful charts beat twelve descriptive ones, and single numbers belong in sentences.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: the recommendation that turns a report into the next piece of work.

lessons.title: The Recommendation That Buys the Next Job

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every report ends at a fork. It can stop at «here is what the data says», or it can continue to «here is what I would do about it».

The first is safer and forgettable. The second is what makes a client think of you as someone involved in their business rather than someone who processed a file for them.

blocks.heading: Recommend Something Specific
blocks.bodyHtml:
Vague recommendations are worse than none, because they signal that you did not want to commit.

«Consider focusing marketing efforts on higher-performing product categories.»

«Stop advertising the bottom four products and move that budget to the two that convert. That's roughly £600 a month redirected.»

The second can be acted on this week, argued with, or rejected — all of which are more useful than agreement with nothing in particular.

blocks.text: A recommendation nobody can disagree with is a recommendation nobody can act on.

blocks.heading: Three Levels to Offer
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Do today — one thing, no budget, no meeting required
  • Do this month — one change worth a small investment
  • Consider — a bigger question this raised, for later

The first gets done and proves the report was useful. The third is where the next project usually comes from, without ever being pitched.

blocks.question: Which recommendation is most likely to be acted on and to lead to more work?

options.label: Continue monitoring these metrics closely over the coming quarter.
Pause ads on the four lowest converters this week and watch the change.
Consider a broader review of the marketing strategy across all channels.
Explore whether customer segmentation could improve overall performance.

blocks.successBody: A specific action with a timeframe can be done without a meeting, and doing it proves the report was worth commissioning. The other three all require someone to first decide what they mean.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask which one a busy person could actually complete before the end of the week.

blocks.heading: Name What You Would Need
blocks.bodyHtml:
If the data could not answer something important, say so and say what would fix it: «I could not separate new from returning customers — if you can export that field, it would sharpen this considerably.»

That sentence is honest, useful, and frequently becomes the next job — without any part of it reading as a sales pitch.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any analysis and write the three levels of recommendation.
Make the first one something doable today without spending money.
Add one sentence about the data you wish you had.
Check that none of the three could be agreed with while changing nothing.

blocks.heading: Follow Up on the Action
blocks.bodyHtml:
Two weeks later, ask what happened with the first recommendation. Very few freelancers do this.

If it worked, you have a result to point at and an obvious next step. If it did not, you have new information and a reason to look again — and either way you are still in the conversation, which is where all repeat work comes from.

blocks.body: Stop at the findings and the report is forgettable. Recommend something specific enough to be argued with, offer three levels — today, this month, consider — and name the data you wish you had. Then follow up in two weeks on whether the first action worked.
